items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: You had the same thing with Malcolm X, always trying to change minds.

ctx.x: Yeah. There were some phrases, when you wrote about, this is from your first edition intro of your Four Lives in Bebop book and you were talking about the new jazz in the 60s and that the musicians broke down tonal centers and chord progressions and pat rhythms, any structure they found inhibiting. And I wonder if in so doing did the musicians expect that the audience was going to stay with them?

I think they wondered about that. They were concerned about it but at this time you’ve got to bear in mind the time that this was. This was a time of challenge, of breaking institutions, of changing society, and it was expected of a committed artist or a committed activist that one would have to change the people to whom their work was pointed. You had the same thing with Malcolm X, always trying to change minds. Martin King was trying to change the attitude of African-American people as well as the white people…

This morning I was reading that comment that I just read to you about breaking down tonal centers and I got this little flash I said, I remember reading something about a liner note that said something about be advised that this record cannot be loved or understood in one sitting. So I went and got my “Ascension” LP and there you were. And you said that this is a “guaranteed soul rinsing.” So I find it interesting what you just said about John Coltrane and trying to make people saints.
